title: Africa 2035: The Boardroom Technology Challenge
subtitle: Major Simulation 2: Trust, Frontier Technology, Strategy, Ethics and Commercialisation

academic_scoring.note: AfriCOIN is the game score. All 15 academic questions are weighted equally for the formal 5% module contribution.

fiction_notice: All organisations, people and events in this simulation are fictionalised for teaching purposes. The scenarios are designed to reflect realistic African business and societal contexts without representing actual organisations or individuals.

primary_sections.section_7: Immersive, Brain-Computer Interface and Frontier Technologies
primary_sections.section_8: Emerging Technology Strategy, Investment and Business Models
primary_sections.section_9: Responsible Technology, Society and the Future of Work
primary_sections.section_10: Technology Implementation, Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Commercialisation

coverage.integration_rule: Stage 3 integrates Sections 1 to 10 and requires students to combine problem framing, AI, data, infrastructure, intelligent systems, digital trust, frontier technology, strategy, ethics, implementation and commercialisation.

core_case.organisation_type: Fictional pan-African diversified technology and services group
core_case.context: Ubuntu Horizon Group has grown rapidly across Africa and now faces pressure to invest in emerging technologies without chasing hype. Its board must manage uneven infrastructure, data gaps, workforce concerns, digital trust, different levels of organisational readiness, ethical risks, local innovation opportunities and pressure to commercialise successful pilots.
core_case.board_mandate: Create responsible, scalable and commercially viable technology solutions that solve real African problems and generate measurable social and business value.

game_rules.answer_format: Single best answer unless stated otherwise
game_rules.badge_unlock_rule: At least 4 correct answers out of 5 in a stage
difficulty_progression: Stage 1 tests technology fit, digital trust and frontier technology reasoning.
Stage 2 tests strategic investment, implementation, workforce and responsible technology decisions.
Stage 3 tests executive integration across Sections 1 to 10 under competing objectives and limited resources.

badge.name: Digital Trust Keeper
badge.unlock_condition: 4 or more correct answers out of 5
badge.tagline: You can distinguish genuine digital trust from technology theatre.

problems.title: The Blockchain Temptation
problems.scenario: Ubuntu Horizon manages industrial equipment handovers involving manufacturers, transporters, port operators, insurers and buyers. Disputes frequently arise because each organisation keeps separate records and no single party is fully trusted by all others.
problems.question: Why could a permissioned blockchain be useful here?

options.A: Because blockchain makes every process faster by definition.
options.B: Because multiple parties need a shared, tamper-evident record without relying entirely on one participant's database.
options.C: Because blockchain automatically removes the need for governance.
options.D: Because blockchain is a form of Generative AI.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. The strongest use case is multi-party trust, provenance and shared records where no single party should control the complete record.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Blockchain can introduce overhead and is not automatically faster.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Blockchain and Generative AI are different technologies.

problems.teaching_point: Blockchain should solve a trust and coordination problem, not merely decorate a digital process.
problems.ethics_flash: If incorrect information is written permanently, who is responsible for correcting or contesting it?
problems.fun_line: If one trusted database can solve the problem, blockchain may just be an expensive group chat.

problems.title: The Blockchain That Should Not Exist
problems.scenario: The Group's HR department proposes storing internal leave requests on blockchain. One HR system already controls the process, all users trust the same central authority and there is no multi-party verification problem.
problems.question: What is the strongest recommendation?

options.A: Use blockchain because all modern HR systems require it.
options.B: Use a conventional secure database because the problem does not require distributed trust.
options.D: Use a public blockchain so employee records are transparent.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. A conventional database is more appropriate when one trusted authority controls the process.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Blockchain is not a default requirement.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Cryptocurrency is irrelevant to leave approval.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Public exposure would create serious privacy concerns.

problems.teaching_point: Knowing when not to use a technology is a strategic capability.
problems.ethics_flash: Employee records demand privacy and access control.
problems.fun_line: Not every spreadsheet needs to become a revolution.

problems.title: The VR Mine
problems.scenario: A mining client needs workers to practise emergency evacuation and equipment shutdown procedures. Real drills are costly, disruptive and potentially dangerous.
problems.question: What is the strongest use of immersive technology?

options.A: VR simulation for repeatable high-risk training without exposing learners to real danger.
options.C: Generative AI replacing all safety instructors.
options.D: A public social-media livestream of emergencies.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. VR is especially valuable for safe, repeatable simulation of dangerous or expensive environments.
detailed_feedback.B: Incorrect. Blockchain does not create immersive training.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. AI may assist training but does not replace the core immersive use case.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Watching is not the same as practising.

problems.teaching_point: Immersive technology creates value when experience itself is part of the learning problem.
problems.ethics_flash: VR assessments should not penalise learners for motion sickness or accessibility limitations.
problems.fun_line: The best place to make a catastrophic training mistake is somewhere nobody gets hurt.

problems.title: The Brain Data Question
problems.scenario: Ubuntu Horizon pilots a BCI-assisted learning tool that measures attention and cognitive load. HR proposes reusing the neural data to rank employees for promotion.
problems.question: What is the strongest governance response?

options.A: Allow reuse because the organisation already owns the device.
options.B: Use neural data for any purpose once collected.
options.C: Apply purpose limitation, informed consent, data minimisation and prohibit unrelated HR use without a new lawful and ethical basis.
options.D: Publish the neural data so the system is transparent.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Neural data is highly sensitive. Collection for learning support does not justify unrelated employment decisions.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Device ownership does not equal unrestricted rights over personal data.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Public disclosure would worsen privacy risk.

problems.teaching_point: Frontier technologies create new data categories that can demand stronger governance.
problems.ethics_flash: Neural data can expose information people may not consciously choose to communicate.
problems.fun_line: The brain is not a bonus data warehouse.

problems.title: The Digital Twin Decision
problems.scenario: The Group manages a large logistics hub. Management wants to test traffic flows, warehouse layouts, energy usage and emergency scenarios before changing the physical facility.
problems.question: Which technology best fits the problem?

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. A digital twin can represent the physical facility and support scenario testing before real-world changes are made.
detailed_feedback.B: Incorrect. Cryptocurrency does not model physical operations.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. A chatbot does not simulate the facility.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Blockchain does not provide the core modelling capability.

problems.teaching_point: Digital twins support experimentation where changing the real system is costly or risky.
problems.ethics_flash: A twin is only as representative as its data. Poorly modelled communities or users can disappear from the simulation.
problems.fun_line: It is cheaper to crash the virtual warehouse.

badge.name: Value Architect
badge.unlock_condition: 4 or more correct answers out of 5
badge.tagline: You can move from technology excitement to disciplined investment and responsible implementation.

problems.title: The Shiny Proposal
problems.scenario: Three proposals compete for funding. Proposal A uses predictive maintenance on industrial equipment with documented failure costs. Proposal B creates a metaverse showroom with no defined customer problem. Proposal C moves one trusted internal database to blockchain.
problems.question: Which proposal has the strongest strategic fit?

options.D: All three are equally strong because they are emerging technologies.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Proposal A is linked to a clear operational problem, measurable value and a plausible technology fit.
detailed_feedback.B: Incorrect. There is no defined problem or value case.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. A trusted single-owner database does not require blockchain.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Emerging status is not a business case.

problems.teaching_point: Investment should follow problem, value, feasibility and evidence.
problems.ethics_flash: Opportunity cost matters when scarce capital is diverted from higher-impact needs.
problems.fun_line: A shiny demo is not a strategy.

problems.title: The Pilot That Worked
problems.scenario: An IoT and predictive-maintenance pilot cuts refrigeration failures by 16% at one urban facility. The board wants immediate deployment across 40 sites, including remote locations with weaker connectivity and different equipment.
problems.question: What is the strongest next step?

options.A: Scale everywhere immediately because the pilot worked.
options.B: Run staged scaling with readiness checks, local adaptation, training, connectivity assessment and measurable success criteria.
options.C: Cancel the project because all pilots are unreliable.
options.D: Replace the pilot with Generative AI.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. A successful pilot is evidence, not proof that every operating context is identical.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Context differences can break the assumptions that made the pilot succeed.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Pilots are useful when interpreted correctly.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Generative AI does not solve the scaling challenge.

problems.teaching_point: Pilot success must be translated into scalable operating conditions.
problems.ethics_flash: Scaling without local readiness can shift service failures onto less-resourced communities.
problems.fun_line: One successful pilot is not a magic passport.

problems.title: Automation Shock
problems.scenario: AI document processing reduces manual administrative work. Analysis suggests that about 30% of tasks in one department will change, but very few entire jobs need to disappear.
problems.question: What is the most responsible management response?

options.A: Announce that 30% of employees are redundant.
options.B: Redesign roles, identify changing tasks, reskill employees and create a transition plan.
options.C: Hide the automation plan until deployment.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Task change is not the same as job elimination. Responsible implementation includes role redesign and workforce transition.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. The scenario refers to tasks, not 30% of jobs.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Secrecy undermines trust and transition planning.
detailed_feedback.D: Too absolute. Automation can create value when implemented responsibly.

problems.teaching_point: Future-of-work strategy should analyse tasks, not rely on dramatic job-loss assumptions.
problems.ethics_flash: Who captures productivity gains, and who carries the transition cost?
problems.fun_line: A job is a bundle of tasks, not one giant checkbox.

problems.title: The Fairness Dashboard
problems.scenario: A loan-support model has good overall accuracy, but approval recommendations are significantly less accurate for rural women-owned businesses because the training data contains fewer comparable historical cases.
problems.question: What should the board require before wider deployment?

options.A: Only overall accuracy because subgroup results complicate reporting.
options.B: Subgroup performance testing, improved data representation, human review for uncertain cases and ongoing monitoring.
options.C: Immediate national deployment because the average is strong.
options.D: Remove all demographic analysis so the organisation cannot see differences.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Fairness requires examining whether performance differs across relevant populations and managing uncertainty explicitly.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Overall averages can hide unequal harm.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Strong average performance does not resolve subgroup weakness.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Avoiding measurement can conceal rather than solve inequality.

problems.teaching_point: Responsible AI requires performance analysis across the populations affected.
problems.ethics_flash: Fairness problems can become access-to-capital problems.

problems.title: Commercialisation Fork
problems.scenario: Ubuntu Horizon develops an African-language AI customer-support tool. A pilot works well with three organisations. The research team wants to release it immediately across 12 countries without validating demand, protecting IP or designing a revenue model.
problems.question: What is the strongest commercialisation pathway?

options.B: Validate demand, clarify IP, define a business model, identify partners, test regulatory fit and scale using evidence.
options.C: Publish the source code and abandon all business planning.
options.D: Keep the tool permanently inside the lab.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Commercialisation connects technical capability to customers, IP, business model, regulation, partnerships and evidence-based scale.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Speed without readiness can destroy value.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Open source can be strategic, but it does not remove the need for a commercialisation model.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Proven solutions can create broader value if a viable pathway exists.

problems.teaching_point: Innovation becomes impact only when it can move beyond the prototype responsibly.
problems.ethics_flash: Commercial scale should not erase local languages or communities that were crucial to development.
problems.fun_line: A prototype is not yet a company.

badge.name: Africa Tech Sovereign
badge.unlock_condition: 4 or more correct answers out of 5
badge.tagline: You can integrate technology, value, ethics, people and commercialisation under boardroom pressure.

problems.title: The 6.2 Million AfriCOIN Portfolio
problems.scenario: The board has 6.2 million AfriCOIN. Proposal A costs 1.8m: predictive maintenance for industrial assets. Proposal B costs 1.2m: VR safety-training platform. Proposal C costs 1.4m: data, cloud and cybersecurity foundation. Proposal D costs 2.6m: high-profile GenAI brand avatar. Proposal E costs 1.8m: permissioned blockchain for multi-party equipment provenance. Proposal F costs 1.0m: workforce reskilling and implementation support.
problems.question: Which portfolio best balances immediate value, enabling infrastructure, workforce readiness and strategic trust needs within budget?

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. This portfolio combines a proven operational use case, enabling infrastructure and cybersecurity, a justified digital-trust use case, and workforce implementation support. It uses 6.0m and directly addresses operational, governance and adoption needs.
detailed_feedback.A: Plausible but weaker. It funds VR before addressing the documented multi-party provenance problem, while the selected VR use case is valuable but less strategically urgent.
detailed_feedback.B: Incorrect. It overweights visibility and novelty without building the core data and implementation foundation.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. The GenAI avatar absorbs too much capital without solving a priority problem.

problems.teaching_point: Board-level technology portfolios should combine value creation, enabling capability, governance and adoption.
problems.ethics_flash: Portfolio choices determine which employees, customers and communities receive benefits first.
problems.facilitator_tip: Ask students why the most exciting portfolio is not necessarily the strongest.

problems.title: The Rural Scale Trap
problems.scenario: A VR and AI vocational-training platform performs strongly in Johannesburg. The company wants to expand to remote communities in Namibia and South Africa. Some target sites have limited bandwidth, shared devices, intermittent electricity and fewer instructors.
problems.question: What is the strongest scaling strategy?

options.A: Deploy the urban version unchanged so all learners receive the same technology.
options.B: Adapt delivery for local infrastructure, enable offline or low-bandwidth modes, train facilitators, measure outcomes and scale in stages.
options.C: Cancel the expansion because rural areas are too difficult.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Equal technology is not the same as equitable access. Scaling requires adaptation to operating context.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Identical delivery can create unequal outcomes when infrastructure differs.
detailed_feedback.C: Incorrect. Constraints should inform design rather than automatically end the project.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Cryptocurrency does not address training access.

problems.teaching_point: Implementation quality depends on context, not only technology capability.
problems.ethics_flash: Digital inclusion must be designed, not assumed.
problems.fun_line: A solution is not scalable if it only works where everything already works.

problems.title: The Data-for-Equity Deal
problems.scenario: A technology partner offers to fund expansion of Ubuntu Horizon's education platform in exchange for unrestricted access to learner behaviour data. The board argues that the deal could help millions of learners and finance rapid scale.
problems.question: What is the strongest board response?

options.A: Accept because social impact justifies unrestricted data use.
options.C: Negotiate strict purpose limits, data minimisation, security, learner protections, governance rights and transparent benefit-sharing before proceeding.
options.D: Publish the learner data to make the arrangement fair.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Social value does not remove privacy, governance and power concerns. The partnership should be structured around necessity, proportionality and accountability.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Positive intentions do not justify unrestricted use.
detailed_feedback.B: Too absolute. Data partnerships can be legitimate with appropriate controls.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Publication would intensify privacy risk.

problems.teaching_point: Commercialisation and social impact must be governed together.
problems.ethics_flash: Who owns the value created from African data?
problems.fun_line: Free money is often not free.

problems.title: The Employee Revolt
problems.scenario: A new AI-enabled workflow could reduce processing time by 40%. Employees hear about the project from a vendor presentation and believe management intends mass layoffs. Productivity drops, unions demand consultation and several experienced employees begin leaving.
problems.question: What should leadership do first?

options.B: Communicate the task-level impact, engage employees and unions, redesign roles, define transition support and involve users in implementation.
options.D: Ask the AI system to write a memo explaining why employees are wrong.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. Technology implementation is also organisational change. Trust, consultation, role design and transition support affect whether value is realised.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Speed without adoption can increase resistance and destroy implementation value.
detailed_feedback.C: Too absolute. The technology may still be valuable.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. A generated memo cannot substitute for genuine engagement.

problems.teaching_point: Implementation failure is often a people problem disguised as a technology problem.
problems.ethics_flash: Workers should not be treated merely as costs to be automated away.
problems.fun_line: You cannot digitally transform people by surprising them.

problems.title: The Final Board Vote
problems.scenario: After several pilots, Ubuntu Horizon has evidence of value from AI, IoT, VR and blockchain projects. However, rural connectivity remains uneven, some datasets underrepresent vulnerable communities, employees fear job loss, a partner disputes benefit-sharing and several technologies require stronger governance before scale.
problems.question: What is the strongest final board decision?

options.A: Scale every successful pilot immediately because innovation leadership requires speed.
options.B: Freeze all emerging technology until every risk disappears.
options.C: Scale selectively, adapt to local readiness, strengthen data and cybersecurity, test fairness, support workforce transition, clarify partner rights, govern high-risk uses and measure impact continuously.
options.D: Choose the technology with the most impressive demonstration.

detailed_feedback.correct: Correct. The strongest strategy combines evidence-based scaling with local adaptation, governance, inclusion, workforce planning, partner alignment and measurable impact.
detailed_feedback.A: Incorrect. Pilot success does not erase context, ethics or implementation risk.
detailed_feedback.B: Incorrect. Zero risk is unrealistic and would prevent responsible innovation.
detailed_feedback.D: Incorrect. Demonstration quality is not a strategic criterion.

problems.teaching_point: The mature technology leader does not ask only what can be built. The leader asks what should be built, for whom, under what conditions, how it will be governed and how value will be sustained.
problems.ethics_flash: Responsible innovation requires attention to who benefits, who carries risk and who has a voice in implementation.
problems.facilitator_tip: Close the simulation with the full framework: African Problem -> Technology -> Value -> Feasibility -> SDG -> Ethics -> Risk -> Implementation -> Commercialisation -> Impact.
problems.fun_line: Welcome to the boardroom. There is no 'deploy all' button.

score_bands.message: You recognise emerging technologies, but strategic fit and governance still need strengthening.
You can connect technology choice to strategy, ethics and implementation.
Strong work. You are making integrated decisions across technology, people, risk and value.
Excellent. You are operating at board level across the full technology-to-impact pathway.

end_game.final_message: The strongest technology decision is not the most futuristic one. It is the one that solves a real problem, fits the context, creates measurable value, protects people, can be implemented responsibly and has a credible path to sustainable impact.
